meta.title: Snowflake: The Year the Market Changed Its Mind Twice
meta.dek: Between November 2025 and April 2026 Snowflake lost 56% because investors decided AI would eat the data warehouse. Then it rose 169% because AI fed it instead. The business grew every quarter of both moves. At $325, what is left to pay for?
meta.type: Consumption-priced cloud data platform (AI Data Cloud)

verdict.sentence: The bears picked a falsifiable fight about agentic AI and lost it three quarters running, but at $325 the price needs FY2032 owner earnings about 40% above my Bull case just to return an ordinary 9%; the probability-weighted case pays [[pw_return]] a year against the 13% hurdle.
verdict.breaks_if: Stock-based compensation stays near 29% of revenue instead of falling toward the low teens, in which case owner earnings never turn positive at scale and no exit multiple on them is defensible.
verdict.bait: Single (A), and it argues against owning
verdict.moat: Moderate; widening in context, narrowing in storage

call: The agentic bear case was specific and it is beaten: product revenue growth went 29% → 30% → 34% → 37%, net revenue retention turned up to 126%, and Ramaswamy says first-party AI contributed about half the acceleration. Consumption pricing was the right model for agents, because agents generate volume. None of that is the question now. Snowflake has never earned a dollar of owner earnings: FY2026 operating cash flow of $1,222M against $1,600M of stock issued, and SBC still ~29% of revenue. I value it on owner earnings, which are about −$0.86 a share this year, and cap the exit at 25× because anything higher implies perpetual growth above the 4.96% ten-year yield. On those terms the Bull alone returns [[Bull.return]] a year with certainty, so break-even and price-implied Bear odds are both negative: no probability weighting of my cases earns 9% from here. The price clears 13% at [[entry]]. Good business, wrong price; the verb is valuation, not thesis.

cells: The 2025 re-rating completes. Snowflake trades near 15× revenue on 29% growth; Databricks is about to raise at $134B.
Dec 3: Q3 beats, but Q4 is guided to 27% growth and a 7% operating margin. The stock falls 11.4% on Dec 4.
Feb 25: FY2027 guided to $5,660M, 27% growth, read as deceleration. Software multiples compress on AI-disruption fears. Mar 31: the CRO is replaced and guidance reaffirmed.
Apr 9: the sector reprices on managed-agent fears — Cloudflare −12%, Snowflake −9%, ServiceNow −7%. The 52-week low of $118.30 prints.

May 27: Q1 +34%, record sequential dollar growth, $6B AWS deal, guide raised; +36.5% next day. Sep 2: Q2 +37%, guide raised again; +16.6%. Oct 9 high of $368.89; Oct 16 −8.4% on sector AI-financing worries.

levers.note: The Base case is carried by market growth, share gain and margin. The Bull additionally needs the attach lever — CoCo and CoWork — to keep compounding and the price/mix headwind to reverse as inference costs fall. Observe is the one lever valued as optionality outside the core. Adjacency test (Zook): Observe shares customers and data gravity with the core but not capabilities, so it is graded a genuine diversification. Built with Claude.

cells: **Switching Costs**, primarily, reinforced by a weak **Network Economy** in the data-sharing marketplace and by **Cornered Resource** in the governance stack (role-based and row-level access control, replication) that Ramaswamy says "take a lot of time to develop." Not Scale Economies: Snowflake rents its compute from the hyperscalers it competes with.

**Mixed.** Widening in context and governance — the semantic layer, Horizon Context and Agent Identity are new and hard to replicate. Narrowing in storage: Snowflake's own adoption of Iceberg v3 and bidirectional Polaris catalogues deliberately dissolves format lock-in. Net revenue retention at 126% is up from 125% but down from 171% at the peak, which is the number that decides it.

The margin is shifting from storage (≈85% gross margin, eroding) to AI workloads (≈55%, growing). The hyperscalers capture the compute layer underneath; the $6B AWS commitment is Snowflake buying scale economics it cannot build. Model providers capture inference. Snowflake's claim on the pool is the context and governance layer between them.

Large enterprises; 829 Forbes Global 2000 accounts produce ~41% of revenue. The job is a governed single source of truth that an autonomous agent can be trusted against. Retention is measured in consumption, not seats, so the metric is NRR at 126%. The last disclosed price action was a margin-reducing mix shift, not a price increase.

**Moderate and genuine, but not wide.** Data gravity and governance make Snowflake very hard to rip out and quite easy to grow alongside; they do not stop Databricks taking the newest workloads, and they no longer protect the storage margin.

model_build.note: Base case. Highlighted cells are inputs; margins and expense ratios move linearly from the FY2027 estimate to the FY2032 input. Two row labels are the engine's generic ones and mean something specific here: the per-segment "operating margin" is the **gross margin**, and "Corporate and other" is **total operating expense**, both on a non-GAAP basis. The exit multiple applies to **owner earnings per share**, not to non-GAAP EPS, because Snowflake's non-GAAP measure excludes stock-based compensation. Owner earnings = non-GAAP net income × 1.30 cash-conversion − after-tax SBC; the 1.30 factor reflects cash taxes far below the book rate and capital expenditure under 1% of revenue. Source: author's model (model.json). Built with Claude.

scenarios.note: Annual return is the price change to the FY2032 value; Snowflake pays no dividend, so there is no yield component. Values apply the exit multiple to owner earnings per share, except the Bear, which is floored at $105 — roughly 3.9× FY2032 revenue plus net cash — because its terminal owner earnings are near zero and a multiple of near-zero earnings is meaningless. The Priced-in and Hurdle rows are solved by the model along the Base→Bull path at a 25× exit. Source: author's model. Built with Claude.

return_math.epv: No positive earnings-power value: five-year average owner earnings are **negative $450M**, so capitalizing them gives nothing. On the kindest cash-based floor — FY2027 adjusted free cash flow of about $1.45B capitalized at 9% with no growth — the figure is roughly $16B, or **$43 a share**, against a $114.7B market capitalization. Essentially the entire price is paying for growth and for a margin structure that does not exist yet.
return_math.base_rate: The Base needs 21% revenue growth a year for five years from a $6.1B base. In the Credit Suisse HOLT reference class, for companies above $25B of market value, roughly 10% sustain 20%+ nominal growth over five years; the best software franchises do it, so the Base is demanding but not heroic. The Bull's 25% is in the top few percent of the distribution. The binding constraint is not growth, though — it is the compensation line.
return_math.year_ten: Still growing, probably low-to-mid teens, on enterprise AI adoption and the context layer. But in every case the terminal multiple is doing the majority of the work, because owner earnings start from below zero. That is the clearest signal that the price is a bet on a re-rating of profitability rather than on compounding.
return_math.note: Computed rows come from model.json; EPV, base rate and year ten are the author's. Built with Claude.
